text: The fuel oil system of the S50ME-C10.7 engine requires careful management of fuel viscosity to ensure proper operation. If the viscosity of the fuel oil is too low, it can lead to inadequate lubrication and potential wear on engine components. Monitor and maintain fuel oil viscosity at the engine inlet between 3 cSt and 20 cSt. Recommended fuel viscosity at engine inlet: Minimum 2 cSt, Normal (distillate) 3 or higher, Normal (HFO) 10-15, Maximum 20. Ignoring viscosity limits can lead to increased wear on engine components and potential engine failure.

chapter_title: 199 04 85-1.0 Insulation and heat tracing of fuel oil piping 7.04
section_titles: 199 04 85-1.0 Insulation and heat tracing of fuel oil piping 7.04
text: Insulation and heat tracing of fuel oil piping is critical for maintaining the temperature of heavy fuel oil to ensure proper pumping. Insulation must be installed only after pressure testing and approval by classification societies. Ensure that the piping systems have been subjected to the specified pressure tests and approved by the classification society. Insulate fuel oil pipes with 20 mm mineral wool and cover with glass cloth. Install removable pads on flanges and valves. Minimum insulation thickness for fuel oil pipes is 20 mm. Recommended heating for pipes is 100 watts per meter to maintain pumping temperature. Failure to properly insulate and heat trace can lead to the inability to pump heavy fuel oil, causing operational delays.

The fuel oil system of the S50ME-C10.7 engine is designed to use both diesel oil and heavy fuel oil. It is crucial to maintain proper fuel pressure and prevent gasification of the fuel in the system. Ensure the fuel oil pressure is maintained at 7-8 bar at the fuel pump level. Adjust the built-on overflow valves at the supply pumps to 5 bar and the external bypass valve to 4 bar. Install a cooler for low-viscosity distillate fuels to ensure viscosity at engine inlet is above 2 cSt. Fuel oil pressure should be maintained at 7-8 bar. The circulating pump pressure should be 10 bar. The viscosity of fuel at engine inlet must be above 2 cSt. Ignoring the need for proper fuel pressure can lead to gasification of fuel, which may cause engine performance issues. Failure to maintain proper fuel viscosity may lead to engine damage.

The use of heavy fuel oil (HFO) with improper specifications can lead to operational issues in marine diesel engines. Specifically, fuels exceeding certain viscosity and specific gravity limits may cause difficulties in combustion and fuel system performance. Ensure that the heavy fuel oil used meets the specified maximum values for density, viscosity, and other parameters. Contact the engine builder for advice if using HFO that exceeds the specified limits. Heavy fuel oil should have a specific gravity at 15°C below 0.991 unless modern centrifuges are used. The maximum acceptable grades for HFO are RMH 700 and RMK 700. Ignoring the fuel specifications may lead to engine deposits, combustion inefficiencies, and potential engine damage.

chapter_title: 198 38 86-5.13 System oil list, consumption and cleaning 8.04
section_titles: 198 38 86-5.13 System oil list, consumption and cleaning 8.04
text: The system oil used in the S50ME-C10.7 engine is crucial for various functions including lubrication, hydraulic control, and sealing. Inadequate oil quality or improper consumption can lead to engine performance issues. Ensure the use of recommended system oils with SAE 30 viscosity and BN level 5-10. Monitor system oil consumption and adjust maintenance practices accordingly. Utilize automatic separators for offline cleaning of system oil. System oil consumption is influenced by factors like backflushing from separators and drain from stuffing boxes. The nominal capacity of the separator must be according to the supplier’s recommendation for system oil, based on 0.136 litre/kWh. Failure to use suitable lubricants can lead to engine damage and operational failures.

The lubricating oil bottom tank must be designed to ensure that the main lubricating oil pumps do not draw in air, which can lead to supply failure and engine damage. The tank must also accommodate sufficient oil volume to maintain proper circulation and allow for the settling of solid particles. Ensure the lubricating oil bottom tank is designed with a sufficient volume to avoid excessive circulation rates and maintain pump suction capability. Verify that the pump suction is always submerged in oil, even during vessel inclinations. The minimum volume of the lubricating oil bottom tank must be equal to the CEAS pump capacity divided by 18. Ignoring the design requirements can lead to air being drawn into the lubricating oil pump, resulting in supply failure and serious damage to the main engine bearings.

The venting and drain pipes for the lubricating oil system must be properly arranged to prevent the accumulation of condensate and foreign particles. Improper venting can lead to contamination of the lubricating oil. Ensure that the lubricating oil bottom tank venting pipes are arranged at the corners or ends of the tank to secure venting at any trim of the ship. Install a drain system for each air venting pipe from the lubricating oil bottom tank. Open and close drain valves frequently during the flushing procedure before initial engine start-up and during sea-trial. The venting pipe routing must be steadily ascending to avoid pipe pockets. The longitudinal inclination must be a minimum of 5° and the transverse inclination a minimum of 15°. Failure to maintain proper venting can lead to contamination of the lubricating oil, which may result in engine damage.

The lubricating oil system must be properly installed and flushed to prevent contamination and ensure optimal performance of the engine. Failure to do so can lead to issues such as high differential pressure and abnormal filter behavior. Flush the lubricating oil components and piping system before starting the engine. Check the cleanliness level of the lubricating oil system using ISO 4406 standards. Inspect the filters before and after the sea trial. The required cleanliness level for ME hydraulic oil systems is ISO 4406 XX/16/13. Flushing time should be expected to be between 15-26 hours. Ignoring proper flushing and cleanliness can lead to high differential pressure, filter clogging, and potential engine damage.

chapter_title: 199 18 11-6.0 Cylinder oil specification and system description 9.01
section_titles: 199 18 11-6.0 Cylinder oil specification and system description 9.01
text: The cylinder lubrication system in MAN B&W two-stroke marine diesel engines requires proper management of cylinder oils to prevent engine wear and ensure optimal performance. The system must be tailored to match the fuel type and its sulphur content to maintain effective lubrication. Ensure the correct cylinder oil is used based on the fuel type and sulphur content. Monitor and adjust the cylinder oil feed rate according to the engine's operating conditions. Cylinder oils must have a minimum kinematic viscosity of 18.5 cSt at 100°C and a maximum of 21.9 cSt at 100°C. Failure to use the correct cylinder oil can lead to increased engine wear and potential damage.

The hydraulic control oil (HCO) system is critical for the operation of the engine, providing low-pressure oil to high-pressure pumps. Proper installation and maintenance of the HCO system components are essential to ensure reliable operation. Ensure the return pipe is installed with a downward slope of at least 15° to allow natural gravity flow. Clean the hydraulic control oil tank before use by removing impurities and treating any rust. Use oil with a filtration rating of at least 3 µm during initial filling and topping up. The HCO tank volume is defined as 10% of the hourly HCO pump flow rate. The maximum pump discharge pressure is 5 barg. Ignoring proper installation and maintenance can lead to pressure buildup, leakage, and contamination, resulting in system failure.

The turbocharger lubricating oil system is critical for maintaining the proper operation of the turbocharger in marine diesel engines. It must supply lubricating oil at a constant pressure, and any failure in this system could lead to inadequate lubrication. Ensure the turbocharger lubricating oil tank is cleaned properly before use. Verify that the tank is positioned at least 1 m below the turbocharger lubricating oil outlet flange. Check that the low-level alarm is set above the minimum level for pump suction. Turbocharger lubricating oil viscosity must be 75 cSt at 50°C. Maximum pump discharge pressure is 5 barg. Ignoring cleaning procedures may lead to contamination of the lubricating oil, resulting in turbocharger failure. Failure to maintain proper oil levels could lead to pump cavitation and subsequent engine damage.

The low-temperature cooling water system is essential for cooling lubricating oil, jacket water, and scavenge air coolers in marine engines. Maintaining the correct concentration of inhibitors in the cooling water is crucial to prevent chemical corrosion. Maintain the inhibitor concentration in the upper end of the specified range. Take weekly samples of the circulating cooling water and test its condition. Every third month, send a water sample for laboratory analysis. Once a year, empty, flush, and refill the cooling water system, then add the inhibitor. Inhibitors recommended: nitrite-borate based Weekly testing of cooling water is recommended Annual flushing and refilling of the cooling water system is required Ignoring the maintenance of inhibitor concentration can lead to chemical corrosion, which may damage the cooling system components.

The central cooling water system is essential for maintaining optimal engine performance by regulating cooling water temperature. If the cooling water inlet temperature is not properly managed, it can lead to inefficient fuel consumption and potential engine damage. Set the temperature control valve in the central cooling water circuit to a minimum of 10°C. If seawater pumps are flow controlled, adjust the setpoint to approximately 4°C above the seawater temperature, ensuring it does not drop below 10°C. Central cooling water inlet temperature must be at least 10°C. Expansion tank volume must be 10% of the total central cooling water amount in the system. Ignoring the cooling water temperature settings can lead to increased fuel consumption and potential engine damage.

The high-temperature cooling water system is critical for cooling the engine components and preventing corrosion. If the jacket cooling water temperature is not maintained properly, it can lead to issues such as cold corrosion and mechanical overload. Maintain the jacket cooling water temperature above 50°C before engine start-up. Use a chemical corrosion inhibitor in the jacket cooling water. Record and monitor the quality of the cooling water weekly. Maximum water velocity in jacket cooling water piping is 3.0 m/s. Minimum jacket cooling water temperature before engine start-up is 50°C. Ignoring proper temperature maintenance can lead to mechanical overload and cold corrosion, especially when using high-sulphur fuels.

The jacket water cooling system is critical for maintaining the engine's operating temperature. If the system does not maintain the required flow rate and pressure, it can lead to overheating or inefficient cooling. Ensure that the jacket water cooling pump is functioning within the specified flow rate and pressure limits. Check the jacket water temperature and ensure it does not exceed the maximum working temperature of 100°C. Verify that the expansion tank is designed and located correctly as per specifications. Jacket water flow must be within 100 to 110% of the capacity stated. Max. pressure drop on cooling side is 0.5 bar. Expansion tank volume must be at least 10% of the total jacket cooling water amount. Ignoring these specifications can lead to engine overheating, reduced efficiency, or potential engine failure.

The starting air system is critical for the operation of the engine, and it relies on the proper functioning of starting air compressors and receivers. Any failure in the compressors or the air supply can lead to insufficient starting air pressure, affecting engine start-up. Verify the operational status of the starting air compressors and receivers. Check the delivery pressure of the starting air system to ensure it is at 30 bar. Inspect the reduction station for any blockages or failures. Starting air compressors must be of the water-cooled, two-stage type with intercooling. Air intake quantity for a reversible engine is for 12 starts, and for a nonreversible engine, it is for 6 starts. Failure to maintain proper starting air pressure can prevent the engine from starting, leading to operational delays.

The auxiliary blowers in the S50ME-C10.7 engine are responsible for ensuring complete scavenging of the cylinders during the starting phase and maintaining proper scavenge air pressure during operation. If one blower fails, the other can still function to maintain operation. Check the operational status of the auxiliary blowers if scavenge air pressure is inadequate. Auxiliary blowers start automatically when blower inlet pressure drops below preset limits. Blowers will operate for 30 minutes after engine shutdown to prevent overheating. If the auxiliary blowers are not functioning properly, it may lead to inadequate scavenging, which can affect engine performance and safety.

The scavenge air cooler cleaning system is designed to maintain the cleanliness of the air cooler by injecting a grease dissolving media. This process is essential to prevent the accumulation of dirt and sludge that can affect engine performance. Inject grease dissolving media through the spray pipe arrangement fitted to the air chamber above the air cooler element. Drain the dirty water collected after the water mist catcher through the designated drain line. The chemical tank capacity for S50ME-C is 0.9 m3. The circulation pump capacity at 3 bar for S50ME-C is 3 m3/h. If the oil content in the drain water exceeds 15ppm, it must not be discharged overboard and should be directed to the oily bilge water holding tank.

chapter_title: 199 20 26-2.0 Control system layout, control units and interfaces 16.01
section_titles: 199 20 26-2.0 Control system layout, control units and interfaces 16.01
text: The engine control system (ECS) for the S50ME-C10.7 is designed with high redundancy to ensure that no single failure can cause the engine to stop. However, if a component such as an engine control unit (ECU) or cylinder control unit (CCU) fails, it may lead to a partial loss of functionality, such as a slowdown in engine performance. Replace the defective ECU or CCU without stopping the engine. The ECS has two engine control units (ECUs) operating in parallel. Each cylinder has a dedicated cylinder control unit (CCU). Ignoring a failure in the control system may lead to engine shutdown or performance issues.

The exhaust gas system may experience excessive pressure loss due to improper installation or selection of components such as the exhaust gas boiler, silencer, or spark arrester. This can lead to inefficiencies in the engine's operation. Ensure that the combined pressure loss across the silencer and/or spark arrester does not exceed 100 mm WC at specified MCR. If no exhaust gas boiler is installed, allow a maximum pressure loss of 200 mm WC. The maximum expected pressure loss across the exhaust gas boiler is normally 150 mm WC. A spark arrester contributes with a considerable pressure drop. Ignoring the pressure loss limits may lead to reduced engine efficiency and potential operational failures.

Axial and torsional vibrations can occur in the crankshaft due to gas pressure loading the crank throw. These vibrations can lead to additional bending stresses in the crankshaft and vibrations in the ship's structure. Install a torsional vibration damper if required based on detailed torsional vibration calculations. Implement the Quick Passage of a barred speed range Technique (QPT) if applicable. Conduct a governor stability evaluation for plants at risk of engine speed instability. The natural frequency of the one-node vibration should be situated away from the normal operating speed range. The first node torsional vibration frequency in the propeller shaft line should be higher than 3 Hz for FPP plants and 5 Hz for CPP plants. Ignoring the need for a torsional vibration damper can lead to significant varying torque and annoying longitudinal vibrations on the engine/double bottom and/or deck house.

The engine's slow down and shut down systems are critical for maintaining safe operation, particularly in Unattended Machinery Space (UMS). These systems rely on independent sensors to monitor various parameters and initiate actions to protect the engine. Ensure that the shut down system is electrically separated from other systems using independent sensors or sensors with galvanically separated circuits. The shut down system must utilize independent sensors or sensors with galvanically separated circuits. The slow down functions are designed to safeguard engine components against overloading. Failure to maintain proper sensor function can lead to engine overload, potential failure, or unsafe operating conditions.

The engine is equipped with various monitoring systems to detect potential failures, including oil mist detection, bearing wear monitoring, and water in oil monitoring. These systems are critical for preventing mechanical damage and ensuring safe operation of the engine. Monitor the water content in the lubricating oil using the WIOM system. Respond to high alarm levels by inspecting the source of water contamination and repairing any leaks. Regularly check the bearing wear monitoring system for high-wear alarm levels. Water activity (a_w) alarm levels are set at 0.5 and 0.9. Ignoring the water contamination alarms may lead to severe damage to the bearings.

The fuel oil system in the S60ME-C10.7 engine is designed to use both diesel oil and heavy fuel oil, but improper management of fuel types can lead to issues such as gasification or contamination. A change-over to diesel oil may be necessary if the vessel is inactive for a prolonged period, especially in cold conditions. Perform a change-over to diesel oil if the engine is expected to be inactive for more than five days or during major repairs. The circulating pump must maintain a pressure of approximately 4 bar in the low pressure part of the fuel system. The fuel oil viscosity at engine inlet must be above 2 cSt for low-viscosity distillate fuels. Ignoring the need for a fuel change-over can lead to gasification of fuel or contamination, which may damage the engine.

The use of heavy fuel oil (HFO) with properties exceeding specified limits can lead to operational issues in marine diesel engines. Specifically, high viscosity and specific gravity can hinder effective cleaning and combustion. Contact the engine builder for advice regarding possible fuel oil system changes. The fuel oil specific gravity at 15°C (60°F) should be below 0.991 unless modern types of centrifuges are used. Heavy fuel oils limited by the guiding specification have been used with satisfactory results on Everllence B&W two-stroke low-speed diesel engines. Ignoring the limits on fuel oil properties can lead to engine performance issues, including deposit formation in combustion chambers and gas passages.

chapter_title: 199 15 05-0.0 Insulation and heat tracing of fuel oil piping 7.04
section_titles: 199 15 05-0.0 Insulation and heat tracing of fuel oil piping 7.04
text: Insulation and heat tracing of fuel oil piping is critical to maintain the temperature of heavy fuel oil for proper pumping. Insulation must be applied only after the piping systems have passed pressure tests. Ensure that the fuel oil piping systems have been subjected to the required pressure tests and approved by the classification society before insulation is applied. Insulate the fuel oil pipes with 20 mm mineral wool and cover with glass cloth as specified. Use steam tracing on fuel oil pipes when the circulation pump is stopped to heat the pipes to the required pumping temperature. Insulation thickness for fuel oil pipes must be 20 mm. Heating to pumping temperature of about 50°C is required for heavy fuel oil. Failure to properly insulate and heat trace fuel oil piping can lead to the inability to pump heavy fuel oil, potentially causing operational delays.

The fuel oil system components must be properly selected and maintained to ensure effective operation of the marine diesel engine. Specific requirements for fuel oil viscosity and separator types are critical for system performance. Ensure that the fuel oil separator is self-cleaning and appropriate for the specific gravity of the fuel oil being used. Maintain the fuel oil viscosity within the specified range of 2 cSt to 20 cSt at the engine inlet. Install a cooler in the fuel oil system if necessary to maintain the required viscosity at the engine inlet. Fuel oil viscosity specified up to 700 cSt at 50°C. Minimum inlet temperature to separator is 98°C. Ignoring viscosity requirements can lead to fuel pump failure and engine wear. Using a manual cleaning separator may lead to inefficiencies and potential engine issues.

chapter_title: 198 38 86-5.13 System oil list, consumption and cleaning 8.04
section_titles: 198 38 86-5.13 System oil list, consumption and cleaning 8.04
text: The system oil in the S60ME-C10.7 engine is essential for various functions including lubrication, hydraulics, and sealing. Improper oil selection or maintenance can lead to engine inefficiencies or damage. Ensure the use of recommended system oils with SAE 30 viscosity grade and BN level 5-10. Monitor system oil consumption and adjust maintenance practices accordingly. Utilize automatic separators for offline cleaning of system oil. System oil consumption is influenced by factors like backflushing from separators and drain from stuffing boxes. The nominal capacity of the separator should be 0.136 litre/kWh based on the total installed power. Failure to use suitable lubricants may result in engine damage.

The lubricating oil system must be properly installed and flushed to prevent contamination and ensure optimal performance of the engine. If not done correctly, foreign particles can enter the system, leading to potential damage. Flush the lubricating oil components and piping system before starting the engine. Check the cleanliness of components delivered from sub-suppliers before installation. Run the purifier system during the complete flushing period. ISO 4406 XX/16/13 is the accepted cleanliness level for ME hydraulic oil systems. Flushing time should be expected to be between 15–26 hours. Failure to flush the system properly can lead to contamination, resulting in engine damage or failure.

The venting and drain pipes for the lubricating oil system must be properly designed and maintained to prevent the accumulation of condensate and foreign particles. Improper venting can lead to contamination of the lubricating oil and potential operational issues. Ensure that the lubricating oil bottom tank is equipped with sufficient venting and that drain valves are opened and closed frequently during flushing procedures and sea trials. Route each vent line separately to open air and ensure the vent piping has a steadily ascending route. The venting pipes should be arranged at the corners or ends of the lubricating oil bottom tank. A drain system can be installed for each venting pipe to allow for the drainage of condensate and foreign particles. Failure to maintain proper venting can lead to oil contamination, which may result in engine damage or failure.

The lubricating oil bottom tank must be designed to prevent the main lubricating oil pumps from drawing in air, which can lead to supply failure and potential engine damage. It is crucial to ensure that the tank can accommodate the necessary oil volume and maintain proper suction conditions. Ensure the lubricating oil pump suction is always submerged in oil. Design the tank to comply with the minimum volume requirements based on the main lubricating oil pump capacity. The lubricating oil bottom tank must have a symmetrical cross-section to avoid bedplate distortions. The pump suction must always be submerged to avoid drawing in air. Ignoring the design requirements may lead to air being drawn into the lubricating oil system, resulting in engine bearing damage.

The turbocharger lubricating oil system is designed to supply lubricating oil to the turbocharger at a constant pressure. Proper design and maintenance of this system are crucial to ensure reliable operation under various engine loads. Ensure the turbocharger lubricating oil tank is cleaned properly before use. Check that the tank is placed at least 1 m below the turbocharger lubricating oil outlet flange. Verify that the low-level alarm is set above the minimum level for pump suction. Turbocharger lubricating oil viscosity specified: 75 cSt at 50°C. Maximum temperature for TC lubricating oil: 70°C. Maximum pump discharge pressure: 5 barg. Ignoring the cleaning process can lead to oil contamination, affecting the turbocharger's performance.

The hydraulic control oil (HCO) system is crucial for the operation of the engine, ensuring a reliable supply of low-pressure oil to the high-pressure HCO pumps. Proper installation and maintenance of the HCO system components are essential to prevent issues such as pressure buildup and oil contamination. Ensure all oil used during initial filling and topping up is filtered through a filter with a filtration rating of min. 3 µm. Install the return pipe with a downward slope of min. 15°. Clean the HCO tank properly before use, removing impurities and treating surfaces as necessary. HCO must fulfil cleanliness level ISO 4406 XX/16/13 equivalent to NAS 1638 Code 8. Pump head (Ph) must be 4 bar and max. pump discharge pressure is 5 barg. Ignoring proper installation and maintenance can lead to contamination, pump failure, and operational inefficiencies.

chapter_title: 199 18 11-6.0 Cylinder oil specification and system description 9.01
section_titles: 199 18 11-6.0 Cylinder oil specification and system description 9.01
text: The cylinder lubrication system in MAN B&W two-stroke marine diesel engines is critical for maintaining engine performance and preventing wear. It involves the use of specific cylinder oils that must match the fuel type and its sulphur content to ensure optimal lubrication. Ensure the correct type of cylinder oil is used based on the fuel type and sulphur content. Monitor and adjust the cylinder oil feed rate according to the latest official guidelines. Cylinder oils must have a kinematic viscosity of minimum 18.5 cSt and maximum 21.9 cSt at 100°C. Cylinder oils are categorized into Cat. I and Cat. II, with Cat. II offering higher performance. Failure to use the correct cylinder oil may lead to increased wear, potential engine damage, and operational inefficiencies.

The low-temperature cooling water system is essential for cooling lubricating oil, jacket water, and scavenge air coolers in marine engines. Proper maintenance of the cooling water system is crucial to prevent chemical corrosion. Maintain the concentration of nitrite-borate based inhibitors in the upper end of the specified range. Take weekly samples of the circulating cooling water and check its condition. Every third month, send a water sample for laboratory analysis. Once a year, empty, flush, and refill the cooling water system, and add the inhibitor. Weekly water samples should be taken from the circulating cooling water. Inhibitors used should be nitrite-borate based. Ignoring the maintenance of the cooling water system can lead to chemical corrosion, which may result in system failure.

The central cooling water system is critical for maintaining optimal engine performance by regulating the cooling water temperature. If the cooling water inlet temperature is not properly managed, it can lead to increased fuel consumption and adverse cylinder conditions. Set the temperature control valve in the central cooling water circuit to a minimum of 10°C. If seawater pumps are flow controlled, adjust the setpoint to approximately 4°C above the seawater temperature, ensuring it does not drop below 10°C. Standard recommended setpoint for cooling water temperature is 10°C. Maximum water velocities for central cooling water and seawater are both 3.0 m/s. Ignoring the cooling water temperature settings can lead to increased fuel consumption and potential engine damage.

The high-temperature cooling water system is critical for maintaining optimal engine temperatures and preventing issues such as corrosion and thermal expansion. If the jacket cooling water temperature is not properly maintained, it can lead to mechanical overload and cold corrosion, especially when operating on high-sulphur fuels. Ensure the jacket cooling water temperature is maintained above 50°C before starting the engine. Install a chemical corrosion inhibitor dosing tank and monitor water quality regularly. Maximum water velocity for jacket cooling water is 3.0 m/s. Minimum jacket cooling water temperature for starting is 20°C, but must reach 50°C before further loading. Ignoring the temperature and loading guidelines can lead to mechanical overload, overheating, and cold corrosion.

The starting air system for the S60ME-C10.7 engine involves multiple components including starting air compressors and receivers that must function correctly to ensure engine starts. The system operates at a delivery pressure of 30 bar and requires specific capacities for both reversible and nonreversible engines. Verify the operation of starting air compressors and receivers. Starting air compressors must be of the water-cooled, two-stage type with intercooling. The flow rate for control and safety air is covered by the capacities stated for air receivers and compressors. Failure to maintain the correct pressure may prevent the engine from starting.

The auxiliary blowers in the S60ME-C10.7 engine are crucial for ensuring complete scavenging of the cylinders during the starting phase and maintaining appropriate scavenge air pressure during operation. If one blower fails, the other can continue to operate without manual intervention. Monitor the blower inlet pressure and ensure both auxiliary blowers are operational. The auxiliary blowers are integrated in the reversing chamber below the scavenge air cooler. The blowers operate automatically based on preset pressure limits. Ignoring blower operation can lead to inadequate scavenging, resulting in poor engine performance or starting failure.

The jacket water cooling system is critical for maintaining the engine's operating temperature. Issues may arise if the cooling water flow rate or temperature exceeds specified limits, potentially leading to overheating. Ensure the jacket water cooling pump is functioning within the specified flow rate of 100 to 110% of the capacity stated. Check the jacket water temperature and ensure it remains at 85°C, with a maximum working temperature of 100°C. Verify that the expansion tank is at least 15 m above the top of the main engine exhaust gas valves and has a volume of at least 10% of the total jacket cooling water amount. Jacket water cooling pump flow rate must be 100 to 110% of the stated capacity. Max. working temperature for jacket water is 100°C. Ignoring these parameters can lead to engine overheating, potential failure of the cooling system, and severe engine damage.

The scavenge air cooler cleaning system is designed to maintain the efficiency of the air cooler by cleaning it with a grease dissolving media. This cleaning process must be performed while the engine is at standstill to ensure safety and effectiveness. Inject a grease dissolving media through the designated spray pipe arrangement fitted to the air chamber above the air cooler element. The chemical tank capacity for the S60ME-C engine type is 0.3 m3. Ignoring the cleaning process may lead to reduced efficiency of the scavenge air cooler and potential overheating of the engine.

The scavenge air box drain system is designed to continuously drain sludge to a pressurized drain tank. Improper connection or blockage in the drain system can lead to pressure issues and inefficiencies in sludge removal. Ensure the drain system is not directly connected to the sludge tank and is designed according to the specified pressure levels. Position the drain tank close to the engine to minimize long piping. Drain tank capacity varies based on the number of cylinders: 0.5 m3 for 5-6 cylinders, up to 1.1 m3 for 14 cylinders. Ignoring the proper design and connection of the drain system can lead to blockages and pressure issues, potentially causing operational failures.

chapter_title: 199 10 06-5.1 Fire extinguishing system for scavenge air space 14.07
section_titles: 199 10 06-5.1 Fire extinguishing system for scavenge air space 14.07
text: A fire can occur in the scavenge air space of the engine, which poses a significant risk to engine safety and operation. Activate the steam fire extinguishing system if a fire is detected in the scavenge air space. If steam is not available, use the water mist system with a minimum pressure of 3.5 bar. As an alternative, deploy the CO2 fire extinguishing system at a test pressure of 150 bar. Steam quantity required: approx. 3.2 kg/cyl. Water mist quantity required: approx. 2.6 kg/cyl. CO2 quantity required: approx. 6.5 kg/cyl. Failure to activate the fire extinguishing system can lead to catastrophic engine damage or fire spread.

chapter_title: 199 20 26-2.0 Control system layout, control units and interfaces 16.01
section_titles: 199 20 26-2.0 Control system layout, control units and interfaces 16.01
text: The engine control system (ECS) for the S60ME-C10.7 is designed with high redundancy to prevent engine shutdown due to a single failure. However, if a control unit fails, it may lead to a slowdown in engine performance. Replace the defective control unit immediately. The ECS has two engine control units (ECUs) operating in parallel. The maximum cabling distance between the engine and the engine room is 100 m. Ignoring a failure in the control system may lead to engine shutdown or performance degradation.

The exhaust gas system components, including the compensator, boiler, silencer, and spark arrester, must be properly dimensioned and installed to manage thermal expansions and pressure losses effectively. Failure to adhere to these specifications can lead to excessive pressure drops and potential system inefficiencies. Ensure that expansion joints are installed to absorb thermal expansions based on calculated temperature increases. Monitor the pressure loss across the exhaust gas boiler and ensure it does not exceed 150 mm WC. Install an exhaust gas silencer if noise levels exceed 60-70 dB(A) at the bridge wing. Check that the combined pressure loss across the silencer and spark arrester does not exceed 100 mm WC. Exhaust gas temperature can increase from 20°C to 250°C. Typical gas velocity through the silencer is approximately 35 m/s. Noise levels at the exhaust gas outlet should not exceed 60-70 dB(A). Ignoring these specifications can lead to excessive pressure drops, which may result in engine inefficiency or failure.

Power related unbalance (PRU) can lead to disturbing hull vibrations in marine engines. The PRU value indicates the risk level of hull vibrations based on external moments relative to engine power. Calculate the PRU value using the formula PRU = (External moment / Engine power) Nm/kW. PRU values for S60ME-C10.7 engine: 1st order PRU for 5 cylinders is 13 Nm/kW, for 6 cylinders is 0 Nm/kW, for 7 cylinders is 5 Nm/kW, for 8 cylinders is 16 Nm/kW. 2nd order PRU for 5 cylinders is 154 Nm/kW, for 6 cylinders is 89 Nm/kW, for 7 cylinders is 22 Nm/kW, for 8 cylinders is 0 Nm/kW. Ignoring high PRU values may lead to significant hull vibrations, potentially causing structural damage.

Axial and torsional vibrations can occur in the MAN B&W S60ME-C10.7 engine due to the loading of the crank throw by gas pressure, leading to deflection and excitation of vibrations. These vibrations can affect the ship's structure and engine performance. Install an axial damper or torsional vibration damper if necessary based on detailed calculations. Conduct detailed torsional vibration calculations for the specific plant. Implement the Quick Passage of a barred speed range Technique (QPT) if applicable. The natural frequency of the one-node vibration should be situated away from the normal operating speed range. The first node torsional vibration frequency in the propeller shaft line should be higher than 3 Hz for FPP plants and 5 Hz for CPP plants. Ignoring torsional vibrations can lead to significant varying torque, which may induce annoying longitudinal vibrations on the engine or ship structure.

The engine's shut down and slow down systems are critical for ensuring safety in Unattended Machinery Spaces (UMS). These systems must be electrically separated from other systems to prevent failures that could lead to engine overload or unsafe conditions. Ensure that the shut down system is electrically separated from other systems using independent sensors or sensors with galvanically separated electrical circuits. The basic safety sensors for the engine are designed for Unattended Machinery Space (UMS). The slow down functions are designed to safeguard engine components against overloading during normal service conditions. Failure to properly implement the shut down and slow down systems could lead to engine overload, unsafe operating conditions, or catastrophic failure.

The engine protection systems monitor various parameters to prevent failures, including fuel oil leakage, bearing condition, and water in oil contamination. Alarms are triggered when certain thresholds are exceeded, indicating potential issues that could lead to severe engine damage. Monitor the water content in the lubricating oil using the WIOM system. Investigate and repair the source of water contamination if the water activity exceeds alarm levels. Water activity alarm levels are set at 0.5 for high alarm and 0.9 for high-high alarm. Ignoring water contamination can lead to severe damage to the crosshead bearings and other engine components.

chapter_title: Bearing failures: When normal readings hide the risk (Gard P&I loss prevention)
section_titles: Bearing failures: When normal readings hide the risk (Gard P&I loss prevention)
text: A bearing failure occurred on a container vessel, leading to rapid heat generation, oil mist formation, crankcase overpressure, and machinery damage. The failure was due to the aft bearing on the upper intermediate gear, which resulted in catastrophic damage and serious injury to a crew member. Implement effective condition monitoring that combines temperature-trend measurement with oil mist detection, lubrication-system data, vibration monitoring, alignment checks, and physical inspection. The aft bearing on the upper intermediate gear failed due to metal-on-metal contact, cutting lubrication to the bearing. Ignoring the need for comprehensive condition monitoring can lead to catastrophic failures and serious injuries.

chapter_title: Preventing auxiliary engine overspeed (Gard P&I loss prevention)
section_titles: Preventing auxiliary engine overspeed (Gard P&I loss prevention)
text: Auxiliary engine overspeed can occur due to setup errors or minor mechanical faults, leading to severe damage. Common causes include mechanical stop transmission failures and verification gaps during commissioning. Run a local emergency stop function test after any control/fuel/governor/actuator work. Make verification of serviced parts a checklist item before start-up. Perform weekly visual linkage checks and monthly torque/contact verifications. Direct repair costs from overspeed incidents average about USD 250,000. Repair periods can range from 22 to 90 days. Ignoring these procedures can lead to severe engine damage and high repair costs.

The low-temperature cooling water system is experiencing reduced flow due to a blockage in the piping, which can lead to overheating of the lubricating oil and scavenge air coolers. Inspect and clean the cooling water piping and strainers. Cooling water flow must be maintained to prevent overheating. Ignoring this issue may lead to severe engine overheating and potential damage.

The cooling water temperature is above the recommended limit, which can lead to reduced efficiency and increased wear on engine components. Check and adjust the temperature control valve settings. Recommended cooling water inlet temperature is 10°C. Failure to address high temperatures can cause engine overheating and damage.

The chemical corrosion inhibitors in the cooling water system are at a low concentration, risking corrosion and scale formation. Add the recommended corrosion inhibitor to the cooling water system. Nitrite-borate based inhibitors are recommended. Ignoring inhibitor levels can lead to severe corrosion and system failure.

The expansion tank is not venting properly, leading to air pockets in the cooling water system. Inspect the venting pipes and ensure they are correctly positioned and not blocked. Expansion tank must be open to the atmosphere. Failure to vent can cause pump cavitation and overheating.

The jacket water cooling pump is not delivering the required flow rate, impacting cooling efficiency. Inspect the pump for wear and tear, and check for blockages in the inlet or outlet. Jacket water cooling pump must maintain specified flow rates. Ignoring this can lead to overheating of engine components.

Corrosion fatigue has developed in the jacket cooling water piping due to inadequate inhibitor levels. Replace corroded sections of piping and ensure proper inhibitor levels are maintained. Inhibitors must be monitored and adjusted regularly. Failure to address corrosion can lead to leaks and system failure.

The seawater cooling system is experiencing high fouling levels, reducing its heat exchange efficiency. Clean the seawater cooler and check for any obstructions in the intake. Seawater coolers require regular maintenance to prevent fouling. Ignoring fouling can lead to severe engine overheating.

The jacket water system is leaking due to a failed seal on the jacket water cooler. Replace the failed seal and inspect the cooler for any additional damage. Jacket water cooler seals should be inspected regularly. Ignoring leaks can lead to significant engine damage and loss of cooling.

The jacket water temperature is fluctuating significantly during operation, indicating a potential issue with the thermostatic regulating valve. Inspect and calibrate the thermostatic regulating valve. Thermostatic regulating valve setpoint should be monitored regularly. Fluctuating temperatures can lead to thermal stress and damage to engine components.

The preheater system is not functioning correctly, leading to inadequate preheating of the jacket cooling water during port stays. Inspect the preheater components and ensure proper operation. Preheating should be maintained at a minimum temperature of 50°C. Failure to preheat can cause cold corrosion and thermal shock to the engine.

The cooling water system has not been flushed for over a year, risking scale buildup and corrosion. Flush the cooling water system and refill with fresh water and inhibitors. Annual flushing and refilling of the cooling water system is mandatory. Neglecting this maintenance can lead to severe corrosion and system failure.

The jacket water pump is operating at a temperature above its maximum rated limit, risking pump failure. Inspect the pump and surrounding cooling system for blockages or failures. Jacket water pump temperature should be regularly monitored. Ignoring high pump temperatures can lead to catastrophic pump failure.

The cooling water system has been contaminated with foreign substances, affecting its performance. Drain, flush, and refill the cooling water system with clean water and inhibitors. Cooling water should be visually inspected regularly for contaminants. Ignoring contamination can lead to system failures and corrosion.

A faulty temperature sensor in the cooling water system is providing inaccurate readings. Test and replace the faulty temperature sensor. Temperature sensors should be calibrated regularly. Inaccurate readings can lead to improper cooling management.

The cooling water system is experiencing excessive pressure drop, indicating potential blockages or restrictions. Inspect the entire cooling water circuit for blockages or restrictions. Monitor pressure drops regularly to ensure system integrity. Ignoring high pressure drops can lead to pump failure and overheating.

The seawater intake for the cooling system is blocked, preventing adequate cooling water supply. Clear any debris or obstructions from the seawater intake. Regular inspections of the seawater intake are necessary. Ignoring this issue can lead to engine overheating and damage.

The cooling water system's expansion tank is undersized, failing to accommodate the thermal expansion of water. Evaluate the tank size and replace it with a correctly sized expansion tank. Expansion tank must be sized according to system requirements. Failure to address this can lead to overflow and system damage.

The jacket water cooling system is experiencing a drop in pressure, which can lead to inadequate cooling of the engine components. This issue is often caused by leaks in the piping or fittings within the system. Inspect the entire jacket water piping for visible leaks and repair as necessary. Jacket water system pressure should be maintained at 3.0 bar. Ignoring low pressure can lead to overheating and potential engine damage.

Corrosion in the jacket water cooling system has been detected due to insufficient inhibitor concentration. This can lead to significant damage over time if not addressed. Check the concentration of the corrosion inhibitor and adjust to maintain it within the recommended range. Recommended inhibitor concentration is at the upper end of the specified range. Failure to maintain inhibitor levels can lead to severe corrosion, resulting in leaks and system failure.

The cooling water temperature exceeds the recommended limits, potentially leading to overheating of engine components. This situation can arise from a malfunctioning temperature control valve. Inspect and test the temperature control valve for proper operation. Recommended cooling water inlet temperature is a minimum of 10°C. Continuing operation under high-temperature conditions can cause severe engine damage.

The expansion tank is not properly vented, leading to air accumulation in the cooling system. This can impair the cooling performance and potentially cause overheating. Ensure that the venting pipes are correctly installed and terminate below the minimum water level in the expansion tank. Expansion tank volume must be at least 10% of the total jacket cooling water. Ignoring this issue can lead to overheating and engine damage.

The cooling water pump is not delivering the required flow rate, which can lead to inadequate cooling of the engine components. This may occur due to pump wear or blockage in the system. Inspect the cooling water pump for wear and check for blockages in the piping. Cooling water pump must deliver a flow rate consistent with engine requirements. Failure to address low flow can result in overheating and catastrophic engine failure.

The jacket cooling water system has developed scale deposits, which can reduce heat transfer efficiency. This is often caused by poor water quality or inadequate chemical treatment. Flush the jacket cooling water system and treat with appropriate scale inhibitors. Regular maintenance and chemical treatment are critical for preventing scale. Ignoring scaling can result in decreased cooling efficiency and potential overheating.

The seawater cooling system is experiencing high fouling rates, impacting the heat exchange efficiency. This is commonly due to biofouling or sediment accumulation. Inspect and clean the seawater cooler to remove fouling. Regular inspection and cleaning of seawater coolers are necessary. Failure to clean the cooler can lead to severe overheating of the engine.

The chemical dosing system for the corrosion inhibitor is malfunctioning, leading to inadequate treatment of the jacket cooling water. This can result in increased corrosion risk. Inspect the dosing pump and lines for blockages or malfunctions. Inhibitor concentration should be regularly monitored and maintained. Ignoring this issue can lead to severe corrosion and potential failure of the cooling system.

The jacket water cooler is not dissipating heat effectively, likely due to a blockage or malfunction. This can cause overheating of the engine components. Inspect the jacket water cooler for blockages or damage and clean or replace as necessary. Jacket water cooler temperature should not exceed the design limits. Neglecting this issue can lead to severe engine damage due to overheating.

The jacket cooling water system has developed leaks, leading to a loss of coolant and potential overheating of the engine. Inspect the cooling water system for leaks and repair any damaged components. Any loss of coolant must be addressed immediately to prevent overheating. Ignoring leaks can lead to engine overheating and severe damage.

The temperature control valve in the central cooling water system is stuck, leading to improper cooling water temperatures and potential overheating. Test the temperature control valve for functionality and replace if necessary. Temperature control valve must be functional to maintain proper cooling. A stuck valve can lead to severe engine overheating and damage.

The jacket cooling water system is experiencing cavitation, which can damage pump components and reduce cooling efficiency. This often occurs due to improper pressure levels or flow restrictions. Inspect the system for flow restrictions and ensure operating pressures are within specified limits. Cavitation can be identified by unusual noise and reduced pump performance. Cavitation can lead to severe pump damage and cooling system failure.

The cooling water system's expansion tank has been improperly sized, leading to insufficient space for coolant expansion, which can cause overflow or air pockets. Evaluate the expansion tank size and replace it with a properly sized tank if necessary. The expansion tank must be designed to accommodate thermal expansion. Improper tank sizing can lead to engine overheating and damage.

The jacket cooling water system is experiencing inadequate circulation, possibly due to pump failure or blockages in the piping. Check the pump operation and inspect for blockages in the piping. Jacket cooling water circulation is critical for maintaining engine temperatures. Inadequate circulation can lead to severe engine overheating.

The water quality in the cooling system has deteriorated, leading to potential scaling and corrosion issues. This can occur due to insufficient monitoring and maintenance of the water treatment program. Take corrective actions to improve water quality, including flushing and re-treating with inhibitors. Regular monitoring of water quality is essential for system health. Poor water quality can lead to severe engine damage over time.

The cooling water temperature control setpoint is incorrectly configured, leading to excessive cooling water temperatures. Review and adjust the temperature control setpoint according to the manufacturer's specifications. The standard temperature control setpoint for cooling water is 10°C. Incorrect setpoint can lead to engine overheating.

The cooling water temperature is consistently higher than the recommended limit, leading to potential overheating of engine components. This can affect the overall efficiency and reliability of the engine. Check the operation of the temperature control valve and the seawater pump. Recommended maximum cooling water temperature: 10°C above ambient. Ignoring high cooling water temperatures can lead to serious engine damage.

Insufficient flow in the cooling water system may lead to inadequate cooling of critical engine components. This can result in overheating and potential damage. Inspect for blockages in the cooling water piping and clean or replace filters as necessary. Minimum cooling water flow rate is essential for proper engine function. If flow is not restored, engine parts may overheat, leading to failure.

Corrosion in the cooling system components can lead to leaks and failures, compromising the cooling efficiency. Check the concentration of chemical inhibitors in the cooling water and adjust as necessary. Recommended inhibitor: nitrite-borate based. Neglecting corrosion control can result in leaks and engine damage.

A failure in the jacket water pump can lead to a complete loss of cooling for the engine, risking overheating. Inspect the jacket water pump for mechanical issues and check electrical connections. Jacket water pump working temperature: up to 100°C. Ignoring pump failures can lead to catastrophic engine overheating.

Improperly maintained expansion tanks can lead to air pockets in the cooling system, disrupting flow and cooling efficiency. Check the expansion tank for proper venting and ensure it is at the correct height above the engine. Expansion tank must be designed to accommodate 10% of total cooling water volume. Air pockets can cause overheating and component failures.

The jacket water temperature is fluctuating outside the desired range, which can affect engine performance and longevity. Check the thermostatic regulating valve for proper function and setpoint. Recommended setpoint for jacket water: 85°C. Temperature fluctuations can lead to thermal stresses and damage.

Excessive scale buildup in the cooling system can reduce heat exchange efficiency and lead to overheating. Schedule regular descaling and maintenance of the cooling system components. Scaling can significantly impact heat exchange in cooling systems. Ignoring scale buildup can result in overheating and component failure.

Inadequate cooling water treatment can lead to microbiological growth in the system, which can cause blockages and corrosion. Test the chemical properties of the cooling water and ensure appropriate biocides are used. Regular testing for microbial activity is crucial for cooling system maintenance. Ignoring microbiological issues can lead to system failures and repairs.

Failure of the deaerating tank can lead to air accumulation in the cooling system, disrupting the cooling flow. Inspect the deaerating tank for functionality and ensure it is venting properly. Deaerating tank must be installed correctly to prevent air accumulation. Failure to address deaerator issues can lead to severe cooling disruptions.

Improper expansion tank design can lead to insufficient pressure in the cooling system, affecting performance. Verify that the expansion tank is properly designed and installed as per specifications. Expansion tank must be open to the atmosphere and correctly sized. Insufficient pressure can lead to cooling system failures and overheating.

If the water sampling protocol is not followed, the quality of the cooling water may deteriorate without detection. Implement a strict schedule for water sampling and analysis. Water quality checks should be done weekly and monthly as specified. Neglecting water quality testing can lead to severe system failures.

Failure of the cooling water heat exchanger can impede the cooling process, leading to engine overheating. Inspect the heat exchanger for fouling or leaks and clean or repair as necessary. Heat exchanger must be inspected regularly for effectiveness. Ignoring heat exchanger issues can lead to catastrophic engine overheating.

Inadequate water treatment can lead to scaling, affecting the efficiency of the cooling system. Evaluate and adjust the water treatment regimen as per manufacturer recommendations. Chemical treatment is essential to prevent scaling. Ignoring treatment can lead to severe cooling issues.

A malfunctioning cooling water control valve may lead to improper temperature regulation, affecting engine performance. Inspect and calibrate the cooling water control valve as necessary. Control valve setpoint should not be outside specified temperature range. Failure to address valve issues can lead to engine damage.

A failure in the cooling water drain system can complicate maintenance efforts and lead to water contamination. Inspect the drain arrangement and ensure proper function. Drain arrangement must allow for proper reuse of treated water. Failure to maintain can lead to contamination of the cooling system.

The cooling water system may experience pressure fluctuations due to improper installation of components. Inspect all connections and components for proper installation and sealing. Pressure should remain stable during operation. Pressure fluctuations can lead to system failures.

The cooling water system may experience inadequate cooling due to environmental factors impacting seawater temperature. Monitor seawater temperatures and adjust cooling system parameters accordingly. Seawater temperature directly affects cooling system performance. Ignoring environmental impacts can lead to overheating.

The cooling system may not function optimally due to insufficient maintenance of auxiliary cooling equipment. Schedule regular maintenance checks for all auxiliary cooling equipment. Auxiliary cooling components must be functioning properly for optimal engine performance. Neglecting auxiliary equipment can lead to reduced cooling efficiency.

The overall cooling system may become less efficient due to the use of incorrect or low-quality coolant. Verify the quality and type of coolant used in the system against manufacturer specifications. Coolant formulation must meet operational requirements. Using incorrect coolant can lead to system failures and corrosion.

The cylinder lubricating oil feed rate is lower than required, potentially leading to insufficient lubrication of the cylinder liners and piston rings. Increase the cylinder oil feed rate Minimum cylinder oil temperature in the tank is 25°C. Ignoring this can lead to severe wear or engine seizure.

Contamination of cylinder oil due to water ingress can lead to reduced lubrication efficiency and increased wear. Isolate the affected oil tank and drain contaminated oil Cylinder oil must have a minimum kinematic viscosity of 18.5 cSt at 100°C. Neglecting contamination can lead to serious engine damage.

A malfunction in the automated cylinder oil switching system (ACOS2) may prevent the engine from switching between high and low BN oils, impacting lubrication performance. Inspect the three-way valve and actuator for faults The ACOS2 system is controlled by the engine control system (ECS). Ignoring this issue can cause engine wear due to inadequate lubrication.

Excessive wear on piston rings and liners may occur if the cylinder oil's alkalinity is not maintained within recommended limits. Replace the cylinder oil with a higher BN oil as recommended Cylinder oils categorized as Cat. II must have a BN of 40, 100, or 140. Failure to address alkalinity can lead to severe engine damage.

The cylinder oil heating system is malfunctioning, resulting in oil being supplied at an inadequate temperature. Check and repair the heating element and insulation Heating element size must be calculated based on engine power. Ignoring this can lead to poor lubrication and increased wear.

Inconsistent cylinder oil mixing ratios can lead to improper lubrication characteristics, affecting engine performance. Calibrate the ACOM system to ensure proper mixing ratios are maintained The ACOM system automatically adjusts mixing based on fuel sulphur content. Failure to correct this can lead to severe engine wear and performance issues.

A blockage in the lubricant filter can lead to reduced oil flow, risking insufficient lubrication. Inspect and clean or replace the lubricant filter Filters must be regularly maintained to prevent blockages. Ignoring this can lead to severe engine wear or failure.

Failure to switch from low-BN to high-BN oil during high sulphur fuel operation can result in inadequate protection. Manually switch to high-BN oil and troubleshoot the control system The engine control system automatically manages oil switching based on fuel type. Failure to switch can lead to severe engine wear or failure.

Incorrectly sized or positioned cylinder oil storage tanks can affect oil supply and management. Reassess and adjust the design of the storage tanks Recommended aspect ratio for tanks is 1:1:3. Ignoring this can lead to inaccurate oil levels and potential supply issues.

The cylinder oil transfer pump is not operating correctly, leading to inadequate oil supply to the engine. Inspect the transfer pump for blockages or mechanical failures Transfer pumps must be capable of handling both cylinder oils safely. Ignoring this can lead to engine damage due to insufficient lubrication.

Insufficient cleaning of piston rings and liners due to poor cylinder oil quality can lead to increased wear. Switch to a higher quality cylinder oil with better detergency Recommended cylinder oils must have high detergency and an appropriate BN. Neglecting this can lead to serious wear and engine performance issues.

The cylinder oil mixing system (ACOM) fails to provide the correct BN due to incorrect calibration. Recalibrate the ACOM system based on current fuel sulphur content The ACOM system adjusts mixing based on real-time fuel data. Failure to correct can lead to severe engine wear.

A malfunctioning lubrication quill may lead to uneven oil distribution across the cylinder liner. Inspect and replace faulty lubricating quills Each cylinder liner has multiple lubricating quills for oil distribution. Ignoring this can lead to uneven wear and potential engine failure.

Improperly maintained cylinder oil storage tanks can lead to sediment build-up, affecting oil quality. Clean and inspect storage tanks regularly Storage tanks should be tall and slim to optimize settling. Failure to maintain tanks can lead to contaminated oil supply.

Incorrect cylinder oil feed rate settings can lead to either over-lubrication or under-lubrication. Reassess and adjust the cylinder oil feed rate settings Feed rate must not be less than 0.6 g/kWh. Neglecting this can lead to engine damage or excessive oil consumption.

Failure to monitor the condition of cylinder oil can lead to undetected degradation, impacting engine performance. Implement a regular oil sampling and analysis schedule Oil condition should be analyzed for viscosity, BN, and contamination levels. Ignoring oil condition can lead to severe engine damage.

A malfunction in the cylinder oil heating system can lead to oil being supplied at a temperature lower than required, affecting lubrication efficiency. Inspect the heating elements and controls for faults Heating element size must be calculated based on engine power. Ignoring this can lead to inadequate lubrication and increased wear.

Inadequate cylinder oil supply due to a mechanical failure in the transfer pump can compromise engine lubrication. Inspect and repair or replace the transfer pump Transfer pumps should be interlocked to prevent mixing of different BN oils. Failure to address this can lead to severe engine wear or failure.

Improperly calibrated flowmeters can lead to inaccurate measurement of cylinder oil flow, affecting lubrication management. Calibrate the flowmeter according to manufacturer specifications Only Coriolis type flowmeters are recommended for low flow applications. Ignoring this can lead to improper lubrication and potential engine damage.

Insufficient lubrication oil flow due to blocked lubricating quills can lead to inadequate cylinder lubrication, resulting in increased wear on the piston and liner. Inspect and clean the lubricating quills for blockages. Lubricating quills are essential for oil delivery in MAN B&W engines. Ignoring this issue may result in severe engine damage or even catastrophic failure.

Using incorrect cylinder oil can lead to inadequate lubrication and potential engine damage, especially during high-sulphur fuel operations. Verify the cylinder oil type against the current fuel specifications. Cylinder oils are categorized into Cat. I and Cat. II based on performance. Using incorrect oil can lead to engine seizures and irreversible damage.

A failure in the automated cylinder oil switching system (ACOS2) can prevent the engine from switching to high-BN oil during dual-fuel operation. Inspect the ACOS2 control system and three-way valve for faults. The ACOS2 system is vital for switching between high and low-BN oils. Failure to correct this can lead to increased engine wear and potential failure.

Insufficient cylinder oil temperature can hinder proper lubrication, especially in cold climates or after maintenance procedures. Increase the heating of cylinder oil and check the heating elements. Cylinder oil temperature is critical for ensuring proper viscosity. Ignoring this can lead to poor lubrication and increased wear.

Inconsistent dosage of cylinder oil due to malfunctioning feed pumps can result in inadequate lubrication. Check and recalibrate the cylinder oil feed pumps. Cylinder oil dosage should be monitored and adjusted according to operational conditions. Failure to rectify this could lead to severe engine damage.

Accumulation of contaminants in the cylinder lubricating oil can lead to increased wear and engine fouling. Change the cylinder oil and clean the filtration system. Oil cleanliness is critical for engine performance. Ignoring contamination can lead to serious engine wear and failure.

A malfunctioning cylinder oil transfer pump can prevent the movement of oil between tanks, leading to inadequate lubrication. Inspect the transfer pump and associated piping for blockages or mechanical issues. Transfer pumps are essential for moving cylinder oil between tanks. Failure to rectify pump issues can lead to severe engine damage.

A failure in the electrical heat tracing of the cylinder oil lines can lead to oil temperature dropping below the required levels. Inspect the electrical tracing system for faults and repair as necessary. Heat tracing is necessary for maintaining cylinder oil temperature. Ignoring this issue can lead to severe lubrication problems and engine damage.

An improper configuration of the cylinder oil storage tanks can lead to inaccurate readings and insufficient oil supply. Verify the configuration and position of the storage tanks and recalibrate level sensors. Proper tank configuration is essential for accurate oil level monitoring. Failure to address configuration issues can lead to oil shortages and engine failure.

Excessive wear on piston rings due to insufficient lubricating oil can result in increased fuel consumption and reduced engine efficiency. Assess the lubrication system for proper oil feed rates and adjust accordingly. Proper lubrication is critical for piston ring performance. Ignoring this can lead to severe engine wear and failure.

The presence of water in the cylinder oil can lead to oil emulsification and ineffective lubrication, increasing wear on engine components. Drain and replace contaminated cylinder oil and check for leaks in the system. Water contamination significantly reduces lubrication effectiveness. Ignoring contamination can lead to severe engine wear and failure.

A failure in the manual control of the automated cylinder oil mixing system (ACOM) can result in improper oil blending, affecting cylinder lubrication. Check the manual control panel and the electrical connections to the ACOM system. ACOM allows for precise blending of oils based on fuel type. Failure to correct this can lead to inadequate lubrication and engine wear.

An improper setup of the alarms for the lubrication system can lead to delayed responses to lubrication issues. Verify and recalibrate the alarm settings for the lubrication system. Alarm systems are critical for monitoring lubrication conditions. Failure to correct this can lead to severe engine damage.

Inconsistent oil delivery during variable engine loads can lead to insufficient lubrication of the cylinder. Adjust the lubrication feed rate settings based on current engine loads. Feed rates should be adaptable to engine load for effective lubrication. Ignoring this can lead to increased wear and potential engine failure.

Overheating of cylinder oil due to malfunctioning heating systems can lead to changes in oil viscosity, affecting lubrication performance. Inspect and repair the heating system for the cylinder oil. Cylinder oil viscosity is sensitive to temperature changes. Overheating can lead to oil breakdown and inadequate lubrication.

Improperly maintained cylinder oil filters can lead to clogging and reduced oil flow to the engine. Inspect and replace the oil filter as necessary. Filters must maintain a fineness of 250 μm. Ignoring filter maintenance can lead to severe engine damage.

Cylinder oil mixing units that are not calibrated properly can lead to incorrect BN levels in the lubricating oil. Calibrate the cylinder oil mixing unit to ensure proper BN levels. BN levels are critical for lubrication performance. Failure to maintain proper BN can lead to increased wear on engine components.

Insufficient lubrication due to a clogged lubricating quill can lead to increased wear on the cylinder liner and piston rings. This can eventually result in engine damage if not addressed promptly. Inspect and clear the clogged lubricating quill. Lubrication pressure threshold: 0.5 bar minimum. Failure to address this issue can lead to severe wear, increasing maintenance costs and risking catastrophic engine failure.

Using a cylinder oil with improper viscosity can lead to inadequate lubrication, resulting in increased friction and potential engine damage. Check the viscosity of the cylinder oil against the specifications. Recommended viscosity index (VI): minimum 95. Ignoring this can lead to increased wear, overheating, and potential seizure of engine components.

Inadequate cylinder oil feed rate can result in insufficient lubrication during engine operation, leading to excessive wear on the cylinder liner. Verify the cylinder oil feed rate settings and adjust as necessary. Minimum cylinder oil feed rate: 0.6 g/kWh. If ignored, this can lead to severe engine damage and increased maintenance costs.

Contamination of the cylinder oil due to water ingress can lead to poor lubrication and increased wear on engine components. Drain the contaminated oil and replace it with fresh, uncontaminated cylinder oil. Maximum allowable water content in cylinder oil: 0.1%. Ignoring contamination can lead to severe engine damage and increased operational costs.

Insufficient alkalinity in cylinder oil can lead to acid formation, resulting in corrosion of engine components. Change the cylinder oil to one with a higher base number. Recommended base number (BN) for cylinder oil: 40-140. Neglecting this can lead to severe corrosion and engine failure.

Improper handling of cylinder oil storage tanks can result in contamination or mixing of different grades of oil. Ensure separate storage and proper labeling of different grades of cylinder oil. Storage tanks should be segregated for different oil grades. Contamination can lead to inadequate lubrication and potential engine damage.

Failure of the automated cylinder oil switching system can prevent the engine from receiving the appropriate oil grade, affecting lubrication. Inspect and troubleshoot the ACOS2 system components. ACOS2 system must operate correctly for oil grade switching. Failure to address this can lead to improper lubrication and serious engine damage.

Overheating of the cylinder oil can lead to thermal degradation and loss of lubrication properties. Inspect the heating elements and cooling systems for faults. Maximum allowable cylinder oil temperature: 70°C. If not corrected, this can lead to oil degradation and severe engine damage.

Inconsistent cylinder oil dosing can lead to uneven lubrication and potential engine wear. Calibrate the oil dosing pumps to ensure consistent delivery. Dosing pumps must be calibrated for consistent delivery. Failure to calibrate can result in inadequate lubrication and increased wear.

Excessive soot build-up due to inadequate cylinder oil can lead to poor engine performance and increased emissions. Review and adjust the cylinder oil feed rate to ensure proper lubrication. Soot levels should be monitored regularly to maintain engine performance. Ignoring excessive soot can lead to increased maintenance and operational costs.

Failure of the cylinder oil transfer pump can disrupt oil supply, leading to inadequate lubrication. Inspect and repair or replace the faulty transfer pump. Transfer pump should be operational at all times during engine operation. Ignoring this issue can lead to severe engine damage due to lack of lubrication.

Using cylinder oil with insufficient detergency can lead to deposits and sludge formation, affecting engine performance. Switch to a higher detergency cylinder oil as per the specifications. Cylinder oil must have high detergency to maintain engine cleanliness. Neglecting this can lead to performance issues and increased maintenance requirements.

Incorrectly calibrated cylinder oil mixing system can lead to improper oil blends, compromising lubrication quality. Recalibrate the mixing system to ensure proper blending ratios. Mixing system must be calibrated for accurate oil blending. If ignored, this can lead to inadequate lubrication and increased wear.

Failure to monitor cylinder oil drain samples can lead to unnoticed degradation and potential engine issues. Establish a regular schedule for analyzing drain oil samples. Drain oil samples should be analyzed at prescribed intervals. Neglecting oil analysis can lead to undetected lubrication issues and engine damage.

A malfunctioning cylinder oil filter can lead to contamination of the lubrication system, affecting engine performance. Inspect and replace the cylinder oil filter if necessary. Filter fineness must be 250 μm. Ignoring this can lead to oil contamination and significant engine damage.

An improperly designed cylinder oil tank can cause issues with settling and drainage, leading to contamination. Redesign or modify the tank to ensure proper drainage and settling. Tank bottom must be sloped for easy drainage. Neglecting this can lead to significant contamination issues.

Poor quality cylinder oil can lead to inadequate lubrication and increased wear on engine components. Replace the poor-quality oil with a recommended brand meeting the specifications. Only use cylinder oils with approved NOLs. Failure to use quality oil can lead to severe engine wear and damage.

Incorrect sulfur content in the fuel can lead to improper matching of cylinder oil, affecting lubrication. Verify the sulfur content of the fuel and adjust the cylinder oil grade accordingly. Cylinder oil must correspond to the sulfur content of the fuel. Neglecting to match fuel and oil can lead to severe engine wear and damage.

text: An unexpected failure in the Engine Control Unit (ECU) occurs, potentially disrupting the engine's operational commands. Switch to the redundant ECU immediately. Each engine has two ECUs for redundancy. Ignoring ECU failure may lead to total loss of engine control.

text: The Local Operating Panel (LOP) fails, preventing manual control of the engine. Switch control to the Main Operating Panel (MOP) or the bridge control. LOP is a backup control interface for engine operation. Failure to address LOP issues may lead to complete loss of manual control.

text: Hydraulic power supply failure occurs, affecting the operation of hydraulic components. Check hydraulic fluid levels and pump functionality. Hydraulic pressure must be maintained at 300 bar for optimal operation. Ignoring hydraulic issues can lead to failure of critical engine systems.

text: A failure in the Auxiliary Control Unit (ACU) leads to loss of control over auxiliary systems. Switch control to a backup ACU if available. Each engine typically has multiple ACUs for redundancy. Failure to address ACU issues may cause auxiliary system failures.

text: The engine interface control unit (EICC) fails to communicate with external systems. Verify connections and reset the EICC if necessary. EICC is critical for interfacing with other control systems. Ignoring EICC issues may lead to a complete loss of integrated control.

text: The power supply for the engine control system fails, risking loss of control. Switch to the backup power supply immediately. Engine control system requires two separate power supplies. Ignoring power supply issues can lead to a complete engine shutdown.

text: The alarm system fails to activate, leading to undetected abnormal conditions. Inspect alarm system components and reset if necessary. Alarm system monitors critical engine parameters. Failure to address alarm system issues can result in unnoticed engine failures.
